Whiting (Merlangius merlangus) exhibits a rapid early life history, with eggs incubated at 8 °C [T = 8 °C] typically hatching after just 9 days [ab = 9 days], a brief embryonic period that aligns with the fast developmental rates observed in many North Sea gadoids. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae, still reliant on endogenous reserves, measure approximately 0.335 cm [Lb = approximately 0.335 cm] at the onset of exogenous feeding, a critical stage where successful first prey capture determines survivorship. The lecithotrophic phase is short, and the transition to active feeding marks a period of high vulnerability. Subsequent growth is rapid, leading to larval metamorphosis, which occurs at a total length of 0.75 cm , a size threshold that signals the completion of body plan reorganisation. These early life stages are strongly temperature-dependent; under the cool conditions of the North Sea, the duration of the yolk-sac stage and the timing of mouth opening are compressed, promoting earlier entry into the planktonic larval community.

Sexual maturation and the onset of reproductive activity in whiting vary markedly between the sexes, a pattern documented from extensive North Sea groundfish surveys. In female whiting, the first reproduction event occurs at 262 days after hatching [tR = 262 days after hatching], calculated from 2005 North Sea data using von Bertalanffy growth parameters, at an ambient temperature of 9.59 °C [T = 9.59 °C]. Males, by contrast, attain first reproduction more rapidly, at 232 days after hatching [tR = 232 days after hatching] under identical thermal conditions of 9.59 °C [T = 9.59 °C], reflecting a faster maturation schedule. This sexual dimorphism in reproductive timing is accompanied by differences in size at puberty; the total length at which 50% of the population is mature is 17.46 cm [Lp = 17.46 cm] for females, whereas males reach this milestone at a smaller size of 15.88 cm [Lp = 15.88 cm], based on the lowest L50% observed in the North Sea DATRAS dataset from 2008. These values are linked to corresponding body masses of 40.47 grams [Wwp = 40.47 grams] at puberty for females and 30.82 grams [Wwp = 30.82 grams] for males, illustrating the earlier energetic commitment of males to reproductive effort.

Reproductive output in whiting, a batch-spawning iteroparous gadoid, is substantial. An analysis of mean sea surface temperatures from the Hadley dataset for the northern North Sea in 1962 recorded an average of 9.39 °C [T = 9.39 °C], a thermal regime under which spawning activity is concentrated. During the spawning season, females produce approximately 3.5 million eggs per year [Ri = approximately 3.5 million eggs per year], a high annual fecundity that compensates for the substantial larval mortality typical of planktonic early stages. This annual output underscores the species' strategy of producing vast numbers of small, pelagic eggs to offset high early-life mortality. The energetic investment in gamete production is considerable, and the spawning period is timed so that peak larval abundance coincides with spring zooplankton blooms. This fecundity, when combined with the species' moderate longevity, contributes to whiting's resilience as a commercially important species in the North Sea ecosystem.

Body size in whiting exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, a feature commonly observed in gadiform fishes. The ultimate total length attained by females is approximately 80 cm [Li = approximately 80 cm], whereas males reach a smaller maximum size of about 68 cm [Li = about 68 cm]. This disparity in asymptotic length translates to a substantial difference in ultimate wet weight, with females reaching a maximum of 5695 grams [Wwi = 5695 grams] compared to 3128 grams [Wwi = 3128 grams] for males. These adult masses, calculated from the 2008 length-weight relationship in a period when L50% was decreasing, are consistent with historical records for the species in the North Sea. The larger body size of females is likely an adaptation to accommodate the considerable reproductive load of batch spawning, as larger individuals can store greater lipid reserves and produce more egg batches over an extended spawning season. This size advantage is also reflected in the larval stage, where the estimated wet weight of a newly-hatched larva, derived from the cube of the length ratio relative to ultimate size, is approximately 0.00022 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00022 grams].

The larval metamorphosis of whiting, a process involving fin ray ossification and the transition from a pelagic to a more benthic-associated juvenile lifestyle, occurs at different ages for each sex under the same thermal conditions. At a rearing temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C], female larvae complete metamorphosis at 59 days , while males reach this developmental milestone slightly earlier at 50 days . This sex-specific difference in developmental rate, emerging well before sexual maturation, suggests an underlying genetic or hormonal basis that prefigures the earlier male maturation seen later in life. Following metamorphosis, juveniles recruit to demersal habitats, where they grow rapidly toward adulthood. The species' maximum lifespan under natural conditions in the North Sea, at a typical ambient temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], has been documented at approximately 7300 days [am = approximately 7300 days], though most individuals in exploited populations do not survive past a fraction of this potential longevity due to fishing pressure.
